Spite Is the Wrong Word

Everybody told Porsche the 968 was a warmed-over 944 nobody asked for. Porsche's answer was to build the two best-driving cars it made that decade — and then decline, almost entirely, to sell them to you.

By Priya Raghavan 20 min read

Walter Röhrl has driven everything Porsche has ever built, most of it sideways. Two-time world rally champion, four-time Monte Carlo winner, the man Porsche hands the keys to when it wants a number that will hold up. He has lapped the Nürburgring in a Carrera GT quickly enough that it stood as the benchmark for two decades.

Asked about the best-handling Porsche he had ever driven, he did not name a 911.

He named a four-cylinder hatchback that cost less than a loaded Mercedes, that America was never allowed to buy, and that most of the automotive press had spent the previous eighteen months treating as an embarrassment.

Part OneThe Family Nobody Wanted to Claim

To understand why the 968 arrived into a hostile room, you have to understand what it was the third of.

In 1976 Porsche introduced the 924. It was, famously and awkwardly, not really a Porsche. It had been developed largely for Volkswagen, was assembled at Audi's plant in Neckarsulm, and used an engine with a great many Volkswagen part numbers in it. It also sold in enormous quantities — over 150,000 of them — and it kept the lights on at Zuffenhausen during a decade when that was not a given.

The 944 followed in 1982 and fixed nearly everything. Porsche's own engine, blistered arches, a chassis that road testers adored. It sold 173,238 copies. For most of the 1980s the 944 was the best-selling Porsche in the world, and it is genuinely difficult to overstate how much of modern Porsche exists because of it.

By 1990 it was old, and Porsche was broke. The plan was a car called the 944 S3. What arrived instead, at Frankfurt in September 1991, was the 968: over eighty percent new or modified parts, a new nose and tail penned by Harm Lagaay, and assembly moved out of Neckarsulm and into Porsche's own Zuffenhausen works for the first time in the platform's life.

The engine was the headline. Three liters, sixteen valves, at the time the largest four-cylinder in any production car on earth — and fitted with VarioCam, Porsche's first variable valve timing system, which later found its way into the flat-six. Two hundred and forty horsepower in European trim, 236 in the States. Two hundred and twenty-five pound-feet of torque at 4,100 rpm. A new six-speed manual, or a four-speed Tiptronic. Engine at the front, gearbox at the back, weight split almost exactly in half.

It was the most sophisticated four-cylinder sports car anybody had built. It went on sale into the worst market Porsche had ever seen.

Part TwoPanned

The reception was brutal, and not entirely unfair.

Porsche wanted 25,000 cars a year. It got 12,780 in total, across four model years — against 173,238 944s. Only in the first year did sales clear 5,000. The 968 base price in America was $39,950, which sounded reasonable right up until you optioned one and watched it walk past fifty thousand dollars, at which point you were looking at 911 money for a car with half the cylinders and, in the eyes of most buyers, a 944's silhouette.

That was the charge, endlessly repeated: it's a facelifted 944 with a new bumper and a bigger bill. The company's own engineers claiming the car was "83 percent new" read, to a skeptical press, less like a boast than an admission of how badly it needed to be believed.

Britain produced the single most damning statistic of the whole affair. In 1994 Porsche GB introduced the 968 Sport — essentially a Club Sport with the electric windows and rear seats put back — at £29,975, some £5,500 under the standard coupe. Buyers responded by taking 306 Sports and 40 standard coupes.

Read that again. Given a choice between the normal car and a cheaper, lighter, better one, the market chose the better one by more than seven to one. Porsche had not built a bad car. Porsche had built a car it did not know how to price.

Part ThreeWhat the Standard Car Already Had

Before any of that stripping-down happened, it's worth stopping on a question the Club Sport's reputation tends to skip past: was the ordinary 968 actually any good?

Because if it wasn't — if the base car was merely a competent thing that Porsche later turned brilliant through subtraction — that's one story. If the base car was already excellent, and the Club Sport simply sharpened an excellence that was already there, that's a much better one. The evidence says it's the second story.

Start with the face, because even that wasn't an afterthought. Park a 968 next to a contemporary 911 Carrera and a 928, and the family resemblance is deliberate — the same slotted nose treatment, the same laid-back headlight angle, the same clean, unfussy tail with its hint of a wing. None of it was inherited from the 944 by accident; all three cars were speaking the same design language on purpose, which is presumably why people who don't know Porsches well tend to walk up to a 968 the way you'd approach someone who looks familiar, trying to place the face.

Under the skin, the engine tells the same story of quiet, compounding improvement. The very first 944, back in 1982, made do with an 8-valve 2.5-liter cut from one bank of the 928's V8 — a fine engine for its day, good for roughly 143 horsepower. By the time that same basic architecture had grown into the 968's 3.0-liter, 16-valve, VarioCam-equipped four, output had climbed to 236 horsepower without turbocharging, and Porsche's own claim at launch was that no other naturally aspirated three-liter engine on sale made more torque. That's eleven years of one engine family being patiently, methodically improved rather than thrown away and started over — the exact opposite of the "warmed-over 944" charge the press kept repeating.

And on the road, before a single Club Sport had left the factory, the standard 968 was already embarrassing more expensive company. In a 1993 head-to-head against a Chevrolet Corvette and a Nissan 300ZX Turbo — the two loudest, most muscular sports cabriolets America had to offer — a 968 Cabriolet quietly won. Testers found it got more confident the harder it was driven, felt light and eager to change direction where the Nissan pushed wide and the Corvette simply bullied its way through a corner, and did it all with a trace of lift-throttle rotation that made mountain switchbacks feel like the car's natural habitat rather than a chore. One editor put it plainly: probing the limits of the open car felt exactly as secure as doing it in the coupe — which is a real compliment, since a cabriolet's extra flex usually costs a driver exactly that confidence. Porsche's convertible conversion, built by ASC in Heilbronn, came in for its own praise as the tightest, most shudder-free job the company had ever signed off on.

None of which is to say the ordinary car was perfect. The same testers who loved the chassis found the cabin snug and the control layout correct but not especially intuitive, and the seats confining enough to notice on a long day. Worth saying plainly, because the case for this car isn't that it was flawless — it's that the bones were already this good, flaws included, before Porsche ever touched a parts bin.

So when Porsche decided to build a sharper version for the people who actually cared, it wasn't rescuing a mediocre platform. It was taking a chassis that had already, quietly, out-cornered a Corvette and a 300ZX on its own terms, and asking that chassis to do the one thing it was already best at, more.

Part FourSo Porsche Took Things Away

Most of what makes a Porsche a Porsche is versatility dressed up as sportiness — a car that will do the school run, the motorway slog, and a Sunday-morning back road equally well, without complaint. The 968 up to this point had been exactly that kind of car: broadly, comfortably good at everything asked of it.

The Club Sport is the one Porsche of this era that walked away from that whole idea on purpose. It was never going to be pleasant on a long motorway haul or forgiving in stop-start traffic — it's genuinely too loud for one and too stiff for the other, and it doesn't apologize for either. What it got in exchange was a single talent tuned so far past anything else on sale that, for a few years in the early 1990s, nothing on the road could touch it in a corner. Point it at a stretch of empty, twisting tarmac and every one of those compromises stops mattering within about a hundred yards.

The Club Sport arrived at the Paris show in October 1992 and went on sale in 1993. The method was the oldest one in the book, and the one Porsche has never stopped believing in: don't add power, remove everything else.

Deleted for the Club Sport

What Porsche took out to make the best-handling car it built that decade
  • Rear seats
  • Sound deadening
  • Electric windows and mirrors
  • Electric boot release — replaced by a cable
  • The heavier wiring loom
  • The heavier battery and alternator
  • One of the two radiator fans
  • The airbag steering wheel
1,370 kg → 1,320 kg DIN unladen weight
A note on that number. 1,320 kg is the DIN unladen figure — the one Porsche quoted and the one nearly every road test since has repeated. It excludes the driver. Weighed the way the EU actually specifies for a kerb figure — fuel and a 75 kg driver included — a printed Porsche model history lists the Club Sport at 1,420 kg. Both numbers are correct; they're just answering slightly different questions. This piece uses the 1,320 kg DIN figure throughout, because that's the one the rest of the world uses too.

In went fixed-back Recaro buckets with backrests color-matched to the paint, a suspension lowered 20 millimeters, and 17-inch Cup wheels. The M030 sport suspension package was optional and transformative — Carrera RS brakes, special front spindles, cross-drilled rotors, Konis with threaded collars up front, coilovers at the rear, bigger adjustable anti-roll bars. Club Sport specialists reckon only twenty to twenty-five percent of cars left the factory with it, and the only way to know for certain is the build sheet, because a great many cars have had it fitted since.

And now the good part.

Porsche understated the car on purpose. Officially the Club Sport was 50 kg lighter, hit 62 mph in 6.1 seconds, and topped out at 158 mph — barely different from the standard coupe. The reason for the modesty was bureaucratic: quote materially better numbers and the car would have needed fresh type approval, which cost money Porsche did not have.

The real figures were roughly 5.8 seconds and 162 mph. Porsche's own homologation paperwork was the last thing standing between the Club Sport and the reviews it deserved, and Porsche shrugged and let the paperwork win.

Part FiveWhy It Handles Like That

The Club Sport's reputation is not sentiment. It is arithmetic, and the arithmetic is unusually clean.

The layout. Engine ahead of the axle line, gearbox bolted to the rear differential, the two joined by a torque tube. Weight distribution lands within a point or two of 50/50 with a driver aboard — the same principle as the 928, on a car that weighs six hundred pounds less. A 911 of the same era rotates around a mass hanging out behind the rear wheels. The 968 rotates around a point somewhere under the driver's hips. One of those is thrilling. The other is repeatable, and repeatable is what makes a fast lap.

The mass. 1,320 kilograms — a shade over 2,900 pounds. That is lighter than essentially every sports car sold new today, and it is the single number that explains the rest. Light cars change direction without arguing, brake without drama, and let you feel what the tires are doing because there is less inertia sitting between your hands and the road.

The torque curve. 225 lb-ft at 4,100 rpm from a naturally aspirated four is a flat, early, entirely predictable delivery. No turbo lag to time, no peaky cam to wait for. On a circuit that matters more than peak power, because you can commit to throttle at the apex and know exactly what will arrive.

The size. This is the one people forget. A 968 is smaller than a modern Golf. On a British B-road or a tight club circuit, that is worth more than fifty horsepower.

Put those together and you get a car that is quick in a way that does not photograph. It does not have a headline number. It just carries speed everywhere, all the time, without ever asking you to be brave.

An honest gap. I went looking for a period Nürburgring time for the 968 Club Sport and could not find one I trust. That is not because the car was slow — it is because the Ring-time arms race hadn't started yet. Manufacturers began quoting Nordschleife laps as marketing in the late 1990s, after the 968 was already dead. There is no number to hold up. There is only the testimony of the people who drove them, and it is remarkably consistent.

A modern yardstick

If you want to know where a 968 Club Sport sits today, don't reach for a Porsche. Reach for a Toyota.

The GR86 is the current benchmark for lightweight, naturally aspirated, rear-drive driving purity, and it is the car every road tester praises for exactly the qualities the 968 was praised for. It weighs somewhere around 2,811 pounds. It makes 228 horsepower from a naturally aspirated flat-four. It sends that to the rear wheels through a manual gearbox.

The 968 Club Sport weighs about 2,910 pounds and makes 236. Ninety-nine pounds and eight horsepower apart — and thirty-three years.

That is the whole argument in one comparison. The formula the modern press celebrates as a refreshing corrective to bloated, overpowered, overweight sports cars is, to within rounding error, the formula Porsche shipped in 1993 and could not sell. The Club Sport isn't a slow old car that people are being generous about. It is a current-specification lightweight sports car that happens to have been built during the first Clinton administration.

Part SixWhat It Feels Like

Owners and testers reach for the same word disproportionately often: communication. Not speed, not grip, not any of the numbers on the panel two sections back — the sense that the car is narrating the road surface to you in real time, through the wheel and the seat, with almost nothing lost in translation. The specific trick the Club Sport pulls off is staying composed and genuinely eager to be pushed at the same moment, which sounds like a contradiction until you've felt a car actually do both. Its natural habitat was always the racetrack rather than the commute, and it never once pretended otherwise.

Two very different cars share this chassis, and they do not feel remotely alike.

The Club Sport is the quiet one, which sounds absurd for a car with no sound deadening. What people mean when they talk about it is that nothing in the experience is theatrical. There is no turbo step, no cam crossover, no drama at the limit. The three-liter four is a large, unstressed, slightly agricultural thing that pulls evenly from 2,500 rpm and runs out of enthusiasm well before the redline, and this turns out not to matter at all, because you are not driving it on the engine. You are driving it on the chassis.

What owners describe, over and over, in almost identical language, is transparency. The steering loads up progressively and tells you what the front tires are doing. The car takes a set early in a corner and holds it. Lift mid-bend and the nose tucks slightly rather than pitching you into a moment. The six-speed's throw is long by modern standards and the shift action is mechanical and slightly notchy in a way that rewards deliberateness. There is a hard, flat pedal box that lets you heel-and-toe without thinking about it.

And the Recaros hold you well enough that you stop bracing with your knees, which is a bigger contributor to going quickly than most people admit.

The Turbo S is a different animal entirely, and reportedly a slightly alarming one. The eight-valve head and the single KKK give it a delivery nothing like the naturally aspirated car — a soft first inch of throttle, then 369 pound-feet arriving in one lump at 3,000 rpm, in a car that weighs 2,867 pounds and has 75 percent of its differential locked. The chassis is unquestionably up to it; the transaxle balance means it does not tie itself in knots the way a 964 Turbo could. But where the Club Sport asks you to be smooth, the Turbo S asks you to be smooth and patient, and rewards you with the kind of straight-line shove that in 1993 was 911 Turbo territory.

The brakes came off a 911 Turbo 3.6, complete with aluminum calipers and cross-drilled discs, and on a car six hundred pounds lighter than the 911 they were reportedly close to unimprovable.

One of these was the best-handling Porsche a world rally champion had driven. The other was the fastest four-cylinder road car in the world. Porsche sold 1,538 of one and fourteen of the other.

Part SevenWhat It Actually Won

Two things, and they are worth more than a lap time.

In 1993 the British magazine Performance Car named the 968 Club Sport its Performance Car of the Year — an outright win, from a title that spent its existence measuring cars against each other on wet British roads and did not hand the trophy to Porsche out of habit.

And then there is Röhrl, who has been widely quoted for thirty years as calling the 968 Club Sport the best-handling Porsche he had ever driven. It is the kind of line that gets repeated until you assume it has been embellished. It hasn't needed to be. It is simply the most useful sentence anyone has ever written about this car, because it comes from a man with no reason to flatter a slow-selling four-cylinder and every reason to say "911."

The company's own hired legend looked at the entire back catalog and picked the cheap one.

On that production figure. Porsche Club of North America and Hagerty both cite 1,538 Club Sports. Sports Car Market and several marque historians cite 1,923, with a year-by-year split of 856 / 536 / 531. A third figure, from a printed Porsche model history, lists 1,371 cars built across 1993–95. The gap is almost certainly a question of whether the UK-market 968 Sport is counted alongside its stripped-out sibling — the two were built on the same line with adjacent chassis numbers — though that doesn't fully explain a third total lower than either. Nobody has settled it, and if anything the disagreement makes the point on its own: three separate counts, all under two thousand cars, for a Porsche now being cross-shopped against six-figure 911s. If you have factory documentation that resolves it, we'd like to see it.

Part EightThe One They Barely Built

Now the other car. The one there are fourteen of.

In 1993 the ADAC announced a GT Cup in Germany for production-based sports cars, and Porsche's competition department looked at the 968 and saw a race car. The chassis was right. The balance was right. The three-liter naturally aspirated engine was not remotely enough.

So Weissach built the 968 Turbo RS, and to homologate it, built a road car called the 968 Turbo S.

What they did to the engine is the interesting part, because it runs backward from where you'd expect. They kept the crankcase and crankshaft — then threw away the sophisticated 16-valve VarioCam head and bolted on the old eight-valve single-cam head from the 944 Turbo S, along with that car's KKK turbocharger and intercooler. Nikasil block, oil squirters, boost held to one bar.

Fewer valves. One camshaft. No variable timing. And 305 horsepower and 369 lb-ft of torque, arriving at 3,000 rpm.

For context: of the two contemporary 911 Turbos, only the 3.6 made more torque than this four-cylinder. The 3.3 did not.

It was built by hand in the motorsport department at Weissach and sold through customer racing rather than any dealer. The base was a Club Sport, always without a sunroof. The front bumper gained a spoiler lip and a second oil cooler, the hood gained two functional NACA ducts, and an adjustable wing went on the tail. Kevlar buckets inside. ABS and power steering stayed, which tells you Porsche did understand somebody might drive it on a road.

Four point seven seconds to sixty. In 1993. From a four-cylinder Porsche that most of the buying public had spent two years calling a warmed-over 944.

Part NineWhy Fourteen

The plan was a hundred cars. Porsche built ten in 1993 and four in 1994, all left-hand drive, and stopped.

Three reasons, and none of them is that the car wasn't good enough.

The price. 175,000 Deutsche Marks — roughly four times what a Club Sport cost. At that number a buyer was shopping against 911 Turbos, and most of them bought the 911 Turbo.

The racers didn't want it either. The Turbo RS was built three times. Porsche's own customer teams, offered a brand-new turbocharged front-engined race car, largely preferred the 964 Carrera RS 3.8 they already understood. Which is the cruelest detail in this whole story, because by several accounts the Turbo RS was quicker — quick enough that it set off a genuine rivalry inside the very department that had built both cars. Two of the three went BPR racing in 1994 and then the program was over.

And it was never type-approved for America. Not one 968 Turbo S was homologated for the world market at launch. A handful have since emigrated — five are reportedly in the United States now — but every single one arrived the long way, decades late.

Porsche built the fastest thing it could bolt to that chassis, priced it beyond reach, sold it out of the race department, and never let America have it. Then it did the same thing to the Club Sport, minus the price.

Part TenThe Part That Still Stings

Here is the thesis, and it is uncomfortable in a way that most Porsche retrospectives aren't.

The 968 Club Sport was, on the evidence of the people best qualified to judge, the finest-driving car Porsche made in that period. It was never sold new in the United States. Not one. The 968 Turbo S was faster to sixty than a 964 Turbo 3.3 and better balanced than anything wearing the same badge. Fourteen exist, and America wasn't on the list.

It is tempting to read that as defiance — Porsche, mocked and cornered, building two magnificent things and refusing to sell them to the people who'd been rude. That reading is more fun than it is true.

The truth is more human and, I think, better. Porsche in 1993 was a company in genuine trouble, running an old platform because it could not afford a new one, understating its own best car's performance because re-homologation cost money it didn't have, and building a homologation special in the race shop because the marketing department had nothing left to give. Every one of those decisions was made under duress.

And what a company under that much duress produced was a car that a two-time world rally champion, given his pick of everything in Zuffenhausen, called the best-handling Porsche he had ever driven.

That's not spite. That's what an engineering culture looks like when you take away all its money and it keeps going anyway. The spite is just how it feels from over here, thirty years later, holding a market listing for a car we were never allowed to buy.

Part ElevenWhat They Cost Now

The four-cylinder transaxle cars spent thirty years as the cheap way into a Porsche. That era is closing, unevenly and in public.

Scaled to the Turbo S so the gap is visible — the three volume cars are genuinely that small next to it. Club Sport and standard-car figures from recorded public sales through mid-2026; Turbo S from its 2021 auction record and the 2026 pre-sale estimate. Exceptional low-mileage standard coupes have twice sold far above the band shown.

For the cars you can actually buy: a decent Club Sport now averages somewhere around $49,000, with the recorded high at $100,800 in June 2023 and the low at $18,285 in October 2024. In the mid-2000s people were selling them in Britain for ten thousand pounds. An ordinary 968 coupe still averages about $33,500, and the cheapest recorded sale this year was $6,188 — which remains, for my money, the best value in the entire Porsche catalog.

Standard cars have also produced two spectacular outliers: a Riviera Blue 1993 coupe that made $123,200 at Amelia Island in 2022 having sold four months earlier for $85,000, and an 8,000-mile Amethyst Metallic six-speed that brought $164,000. Rare color plus three pedals plus low miles is its own market.

And then March 2026 happened, and it is the most interesting thing to occur to this model in thirty years.

The Turbo S carried a $900,000–$1.2M estimate and would have been the first front-engined Porsche to sell publicly for seven figures. It failed to meet reserve. The one-of-three Turbo RS, at the other house on the same weekend, sold — and at $775,000 is now the highest recorded 968 sale of any kind.

Which is a fittingly awkward ending for this car. Offered the chance to make the 968 a millionaire's model at last, the collector market looked at the rarest and best of them, and passed. Thirty-three years on, the 968 is still the Porsche that doesn't quite get invited.

Part TwelveThe Last of the Line

Production ended in 1995. It ended the same year as the 928, and with it ended the whole front-engined transaxle idea that had started with the 924 nineteen years earlier. Porsche would not build another front-engined car until the Cayenne in 2003, and that is a different kind of story entirely.

What replaced the 968 was the Boxster, which was mid-engined, cheaper to build, hugely successful, and saved the company. Nobody sensible argues Porsche made the wrong call.

But something specific went out of the building in 1995 and has never quite come back. A modern Cayman GT4 is a faster car by every measure and probably a better one. It also carries the better part of a hundred kilos more, costs far more in real terms, and arrives with a lap time attached before you have turned a wheel.

The 968 Club Sport arrived with a window crank and a set of Recaros and a total absence of anything to show off. You had to drive it to find out. Almost nobody did — Porsche saw to that — and the ones who did have spent thirty years telling everyone else, and being politely ignored.

The Verdict

The 968 Club Sport is the best-driving Porsche most people have never sat in, and the market has finally started agreeing at roughly the speed of a glacier. The Turbo S is one of the rarest road cars Weissach ever signed off on and, on the numbers, one of the most quietly outrageous — a 305-horsepower eight-valve four that out-torqued a 911 Turbo and hit sixty in 4.7 seconds in the same year Bill Clinton was inaugurated.

Porsche built both while insolvent, understated one of them on purpose, sold fourteen of the other, and let America have neither.

Ask Walter Röhrl which Porsche handles best. He already answered. Nobody listened then, either.
